summaries.summary: Prior knowledge in NLP includes category-indicating words like NBA, player, and basketball and sentiment words like terrible, boring, messing, perfect, exciting, and moving.
Prior studies leverage prior knowledge to label data, encode parameter priors, formalize variables and dependencies, or control distributions over latent output variables.
Bias in supplied prior knowledge is rarely addressed, and a baseball-hockey example shows uneven feature knowledge may mislead the model toward baseball.
The paper studies robustness in Generalized Expectation Criteria BIBREF7 using auxiliary regularization terms and finds neutral feature words can boost performance remarkably.
The proposed approach does not need manual annotation to label neutral feature words.
Three regularization terms are explored: neutral features, maximum entropy of class distribution, and KL divergence between reference and predicted class distribution.
The paragraph introduces the main contributions of this work.
Section 2 describes generalized expectation criteria and regularization terms, Section 3 conducts experiments, Section 4 surveys related work, and Section 5 summarizes.
The robustness problem is addressed on top of GE-FL BIBREF0, where manually provided labeled features are strong indicators of specific classes.
Generalized expectation (GE) criteria BIBREF7 directly constrain models toward preferred directions, such as a pre-specified class distribution.
A GE term expresses preferences on constraint functions about the model's expectation using $G({m x}, y)$, $p_	heta (y|m x)$, $	ilde{p}({m x})$, and $S$.
The GE term is expressed as $$S(E_{\tilde{p}({\rm x})}[E_{p_\theta (y|{\rm x})}[G({\rm x}, y)]])$$ (Eq. 4).
Druck et al. ge-fl proposed GE-FL to learn from labeled features $K$ using divergence between $\hat{p}(y| x_k)$ and $p_\theta (y | x_k)$.
The GE-FL objective is $$\mathcal {O} = \sum _{k \in K} KL(\hat{p}(y|x_k) || p_\theta (y | x_k)) + \sum _{y,i} \frac{\theta _{yi}^2}{2 \sigma ^2}$$ (Eq. 6).
$\theta _{yi}$ indicates word $i$'s importance to class $y$, and $p_\theta (y | x_k)$ is expressed using $C_k$, $p_\theta (y|{\rm x})$, and $I(x_k)$.
$I(x_k)$ is 1 if feature $k$ occurs, $C_k$ counts instances with feature $k$, and $p_\theta (y|{\rm x})$ takes a softmax form.
L-BFGS can be used for parameter estimation to solve the optimization problem.
In GE, the term is obtained by setting $G({\rm x}, y) = \frac{1}{C_k} \vec{I} (y)I(x_k)$, where $\vec{I}(y)$ is an indicator vector.
GE-FL performs well with unbiased prior knowledge but requires comparable labeled features per class, and three terms are shown to make the model more robust.
Neutral features are frequent, noninformative words like player, and a uniform preference distribution prevents bias toward classes with dominate labeled features.
For neutral features $K^{^{\prime }}$, the uniform distribution is $\hat{p}_u(y|x_k) = \frac{1}{|C|}, k \in K^{^{\prime }}$, where $|C|$ is the number of classes.
The objective with the neutral-feature term is $$\mathcal {O}_{NE} = \mathcal {O} + \sum _{k \in K^{^{\prime }}} KL(\hat{p}_u(y|x_k) || p_\theta (y | x_k)).$$ (Eq. 9).
Neutral features need no manual annotation, and taking the most common features as neutral features works successfully in experiments.
Another way to prevent drift is constraining predicted class distribution on unlabeled data using the maximum entropy principle when class distribution knowledge is lacking.
The maximum entropy objective is $$\mathcal {O}_{ME} = \mathcal {O} + \lambda \sum _{y} p(y) \log p(y)$$ (Eq. 11).
$p(y)$ is the predicted class distribution, and $\lambda $ can be tuned, with $\lambda = \beta |K|$ set proportional to total labeled features.
The maximum entropy term is derived by setting $G({\rm x}, y) = \vec{I}(y)$ and using a maximum entropy form for $S$.
When corpus knowledge allows rough class distribution estimation, KL divergence between predicted and reference class distributions is introduced into the objective function.
Given preference class distribution $\hat{p}(y)$, the objective function is modified.
The KL objective is $$\mathcal {O}_{KL} &= \mathcal {O} + \lambda KL(\hat{p}(y) || p(y))$$ (Eq. 13).
Similarly, $\lambda = \beta |K|$ is set.
The divergence term is derived with $G({\rm x}, y) = \vec{I}(y)$ and $S(\hat{p}, p) = \sum _i \hat{p}_i \log \frac{\hat{p}_i}{p_i}$, involving the reference class distribution.

Experiments justify the approach under unbalanced labeled features or class distribution, test $\lambda $ with KL divergence, and evaluate 9 text classification datasets with $\lambda = 5|K|$ and GE-FL BIBREF0 baseline.
Evaluation uses datasets spanning sentiment, web-page, science, medical and healthcare, with bag-of-words features, stopword removal, and feature labels instead of document labels.
The movie dataset classifies reviews as positive or negtive, supports unbalanced settings by removing positive documents, and uses 10-fold cross validation.
Labeled features are obtained by information gain selecting the top 20 per class or by LDA BIBREF9 selecting probable topic features sorted by $P(w_i|t_j)$.
A heuristic estimates labeled-feature reference distributions, assigning $\frac{0.9}{n}$ to associated classes and $\frac{0.1}{|C| - n}$ to other classes.
Neutral features are the most frequent words after stopword removal, have uniform reference distributions, and use the top 10 frequent words in all experiments.
This section evaluates unbalanced knowledge across categories using labeled features obtained through information gain in two settings.
Setting (a) selects $t \in [1, 20]$ features for one class and one for the other on the balanced movie dataset (positive:negative=1:1).
Setting (b) resembles (a) but uses an unbalanced dataset made by randomly removing 75% positive documents (positive:negative=1:4).
Figure 1 shows Maximum entropy principle improves only the balanced case because maximum entropy favors uniform distribution.
Neutral features perform similarly to maximum entropy, with accuracy decreasing slowly for $t>4$ as the model gradually biases like GE-FL.
KL divergence of class distribution performs much better than GE-FL on balanced and unbalanced datasets, effectively controlling unbalance in labeled features and the dataset.
This section compares with the baseline when labeled features are balanced, using information gain and two experimental settings.
Setting (a) selects $t \in [1, 20]$ features per class on the original balanced movie dataset (positive:negtive=1:1).
Setting (b) resembles (a) but uses an unbalanced class distribution by randomly removing 75% positive documents (positive:negative=1:4).
Figure 2 shows little difference on balanced data, while KL divergence is much better on unbalanced data and maximum entropy and neutral features are much worse.
Movie datasets with class distributions 1:2, 1:3, 1:4 are constructed by removing 50%, 67%, 75% positive documents, with balanced and unbalanced labeled features tested in Figure 3.
Figure 3 (a) shows little difference when balanced, but more unbalanced distributions make KL divergence increase remarkably while neutral features and maximum entropy decrease significantly.
Figure 3 (b) shows that with unbalanced labeled features, the methods significantly outperform GE-FL, and KL divergence robustly controls both dataset and feature unbalance.
This section presents $\lambda $'s influence on KL divergence by tuning $\beta $ in $\lambda = \beta |K|$, where $\beta = 0$ makes the model GE-FL.
Setting (a) selects $t \in [1, 20]$ features for one class and one for the other on the original balanced movie dataset (positive:negative=1:1).
Figure 4 shows $\lambda $ reflects regularization strength, with the model moving closer to preferences as $\lambda $ increases in both cases.
The methods are compared with GE-FL on all 9 datasets using LDA-selected labeled features, enabling classification models without instance annotation.
Table 1 shows the three methods significantly outperform GE-FL, with neutral features better on 7 of the 9 datasets, maximum entropy on 8, and KL divergence on 7.
LDA selects predictive features without considering class balance, so GE-FL suffers while auxiliary regularization terms control bias and significantly promote the model.
Related work surveys two lines: using prior knowledge to label unlabeled instances before standard learning, and constraining the model directly with prior knowledge.
Liu et al.text, Chang et al.guiding, and Daumé daume2008cross use labeled features, constraints, and cross task knowledge constraints to annotate or select unlabeled data.

MaCallum et al.gec, Graça et al.pr, Druck et al.ge-fl, Andrzejewski et al.andrzejewski2011framework, Altendorf et al.altendorf2012learning, and Chen et al.chen2013leveraging constrain models with prior knowledge.
Mann and McCallum simple,generalized incorporated labeled features and class distribution into GE-FL but did not investigate the robustness problem addressed here.
Raghavan et al.feedback used interlaced feedback on instances and features, while Druck et al.active solicited feature labels and used GE-FL.

This paper investigates robustly leveraging prior knowledge in learning models, proposes three regularization terms on generalized expectation criteria, and reports improved, more robust performance against baselines.
Incorporating neutral features is the simplest regularization, requires no GE-FL modification, but Figure 1 (a) shows it cannot handle extremely unbalanced labeled features.
The maximum entropy regularization term shows strong ability in controlling unbalance.
This method needs no extra knowledge but assumes uniformly distributed categories, degrading performance when violated, as shown in Figure 1 (b), Figure 2 (b), and Figure 3 (a).
KL divergence performs much better on unbalanced corpora by using the reference class distribution without assumptions, suggesting additional knowledge benefits the model.
KL divergence requires the true class distribution, but rough estimates suffice; with true distribution 1:2 and references 1:1.5/1:2/1:2.5, accuracy is 0.755/0.756/0.760.
